title: Data Warehousing and Dimensional Modelling
subtitle: Design star schemas the Kimball way, keep history with slowly changing dimensions, and build and load a working warehouse in DuckDB with SQL you run.
outcomes: Explain how analytical workloads differ from transactional ones, and why warehouses store data by column
Design a dimensional model with Kimball's four steps: business process, grain, dimensions and facts
Keep history with type 1 and type 2 slowly changing dimensions, and find the right version when loading facts
Choose between star and snowflake designs, and build aggregates and partitioned Parquet that reconcile with the base facts
Write incremental, idempotent loads with unknown and inferred members, and explain where lakehouse table formats fit
prerequisites: SQL for Data Analysis with DataGrip, or the same SQL: joins, GROUP BY, CTEs and window functions. Data Engineering Foundations: Batch and Streaming Pipelines helps but isn't required. Install Python 3.10 or later and the duckdb package (pip install duckdb); PostgreSQL is optional. Analytics Engineering with dbt and DuckDB and Enterprise Data and ML Platforms make good next steps.
description:
A data warehouse turns the records a business keeps into answers it can trust: revenue by region and month, stock that's about to run out, customers as they were last year and as they are today. This course teaches the design behind that, the dimensional modelling Ralph Kimball made standard, and has you build it. You'll start from a co-op's normalised sales database and see why analysts need a different shape, then declare a grain, design facts and dimensions with surrogate keys, keep history with type 1 and type 2 slowly changing dimensions, and compare star and snowflake schemas, aggregate tables and partitioned Parquet files.

Every module has a lab in DuckDB, a free analytical database that runs on any laptop with no server, with starter files and data that are identical on every computer, so your results can be checked to the penny. You'll write the SQL that builds the star, applies customer changes and looks up the right version of each customer, then a Python loader that's incremental, idempotent and audited. The last module places all of this in today's stack of cloud warehouses, ELT and lakehouse table formats such as Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, and the capstone has you design and build a medicine-supply warehouse for rural clinics with three kinds of fact table.

modules.title: Analytical workloads and the data warehouse
modules.summary: Why the database that records sales is the wrong shape for analysing them: OLTP versus OLAP, what a data warehouse is and how it's built, and how columnar engines such as DuckDB run analytical queries.

lessons.title: OLTP and OLAP: two workloads, two designs
objectives: Contrast transactional and analytical workloads
Explain why normalised schemas suit recording data but not analysing it
key_points: Online transaction processing (OLTP) systems, such as a shop's tills or an order website, run many small reads and writes that each touch a few rows found by key, and must stay correct while many users change data at once.
Online analytical processing (OLAP) runs fewer, larger queries that scan and summarise many rows, such as revenue by region and month, and mostly reads data rather than changing it.

OLTP schemas are normalised, typically to third normal form, so each fact is stored once and updates can't contradict each other; answering a business question from them needs many joins across many tables.
Running heavy analysis on the operational database slows the application people depend on, and that database usually keeps only current values, not the history analysts need.
A data warehouse is a separate database designed for analysis: data is copied from the source systems, cleaned, integrated and reshaped for querying, and kept with its history.

lessons.title: What a data warehouse is, and how it's built
objectives: Describe the layers data passes through on its way into a warehouse
Compare the Inmon and Kimball approaches, and ETL with ELT
key_points: Bill Inmon's classic definition calls a warehouse subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile: organised around business subjects, consistent across sources, kept over time, and added to rather than overwritten.

Inmon's approach builds a normalised enterprise warehouse first and feeds departmental data marts from it; Ralph Kimball's builds dimensional models one business process at a time, tied together by shared (conformed) dimensions in what he calls the bus architecture.

Data usually passes through layers: staging holds raw extracts as they arrived, an integration layer cleans them and matches keys across sources, and a presentation layer of dimensional models is what people and BI tools query.

ETL transforms data before loading it into the warehouse; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse with SQL, which is now common because cloud warehouses scale storage and compute separately.
A warehouse is only trusted if its numbers reconcile with the source systems, so every load is checked with row counts and control totals, such as the sum of net sales, against the source.

lessons.title: Columnar storage and how analytical engines run queries
objectives: Explain why column-oriented storage speeds up analytical queries
Read a DuckDB query plan and a Parquet file's metadata
key_points: Row stores such as PostgreSQL keep each row's values together, which suits reading or updating whole records; column stores keep each column's values together, so a query reads only the columns it uses.
Values in one column are alike, so they compress well with encodings such as dictionary and run-length encoding, and the engine reads less data from disk.
Columnar engines keep the minimum and maximum of each block of rows, called zone maps or, in Parquet, row-group statistics, and skip any block whose range can't match a query's filter.
Vectorised execution, as in DuckDB, processes a batch of values from a column at a time instead of one row at a time, which makes better use of modern CPUs.

DuckDB is an in-process analytical database: it runs inside Python or its command-line tool with no server, reads CSV and Parquet files directly, and EXPLAIN shows the operators, such as SEQ_SCAN, HASH_JOIN and HASH_GROUP_BY, that will run a query.

Apache Parquet is an open columnar file format: a file is split into row groups, each with one column chunk per column and that chunk's statistics, and most warehouse and lakehouse tools read and write it.

"""Write the Millbrook Co-op's source data to the data folder as CSV files.

The co-op has three stores and an online shop. Only random.Random(42).random() is used,
so every computer and every Python 3 version writes exactly the same rows.

Run:  python make_data.py
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path("data")
rng = random.Random(42)


def pick(seq):
    return seq[int(rng.random() * len(seq))]


def between(lo, hi):
    return lo + int(rng.random() * (hi - lo + 1))


STORES = [(1, "Millbrook High Street", "Millbrook", "North", "2015-04-01"),
          (2, "Eastholm Market", "Eastholm", "East", "2018-09-15"),
          (3, "Westcombe Depot", "Westcombe", "West", "2021-03-01")]
CATEGORIES = [(1, "Seeds", "Garden"), (2, "Tools", "Garden"), (3, "Feed", "Farm"),
              (4, "Fencing", "Farm"), (5, "Produce", "Food"), (6, "Dairy", "Food")]
PRODUCTS = [  # product_id, sku, name, category_id, list price (multiples of 0.10)
    (1, "SD-001", "Carrot seeds", 1, "2.50"), (2, "SD-002", "Kale seeds", 1, "2.80"),
    (3, "SD-003", "Seed potatoes 5kg", 1, "7.90"), (4, "TL-001", "Spade", 2, "24.90"),
    (5, "TL-002", "Pruning shears", 2, "14.50"), (6, "TL-003", "Wheelbarrow", 2, "69.00"),
    (7, "FD-001", "Layer pellets 20kg", 3, "15.60"), (8, "FD-002", "Sheep nuts 25kg", 3, "13.20"),
    (9, "FD-003", "Calf milk replacer", 3, "32.40"), (10, "FN-001", "Fence post 1.8m", 4, "4.20"),
    (11, "FN-002", "Barbed wire 200m", 4, "38.50"), (12, "FN-003", "Electric fence tape", 4, "9.70"),
    (13, "PR-001", "Apples 1kg", 5, "2.20"), (14, "PR-002", "Potatoes 2.5kg", 5, "2.90"),
    (15, "PR-003", "Free-range eggs x12", 5, "3.60"), (16, "DY-001", "Whole milk 2l", 6, "1.80"),
    (17, "DY-002", "Cheddar 400g", 6, "4.40"), (18, "DY-003", "Butter 250g", 6, "2.60")]
FIRST = ["Amara", "Kofi", "Lena", "Ravi", "Sofia", "Mateo", "Aiko", "Tomasz", "Ngozi", "Liam",
         "Priya", "Jonas", "Fatima", "Hugo", "Mei", "Omar", "Elif", "Arjun", "Nadia", "Rhys"]
LAST = ["Okafor", "Mensah", "Novak", "Patel", "Rossi", "Silva", "Tanaka", "Kowalski", "Eze", "Murphy",
        "Singh", "Berg", "Haddad", "Laurent", "Chen", "Farah", "Yilmaz", "Rao", "Petrova", "Evans"]
TOWNS = ["Millbrook", "Eastholm", "Westcombe", "Brackenridge"]
HOME_STORE = {"Millbrook": 1, "Eastholm": 2, "Westcombe": 3}


def write(name, header, rows):
    with open(OUT / name, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(header)
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"{name}: {len(rows)} rows")


def customers():
    rows = []
    for cid in range(1, 41):
        first, last = pick(FIRST), pick(LAST)
        rows.append([cid, first, last, f"{first}.{last}{cid}@example.org".lower(), pick(TOWNS),
                     pick(["member", "member", "member", "trade", "guest"]),
                     (date(2023, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=between(0, 700))).isoformat()])
    return rows


def changed_customers(rows):
    """The customer extract on 2025-07-01: moves, a segment change, corrections and two new customers."""
    new = [list(r) for r in rows]
    by_id = {r[0]: r for r in new}
    for cid in (3, 17, 29):  # moved town
        r = by_id[cid]
        r[4] = TOWNS[(TOWNS.index(r[4]) + 1) % len(TOWNS)]
    by_id[12][5] = "trade" if by_id[12][5] != "trade" else "member"  # changed segment
    for cid in (8, 21):  # email address corrected
        by_id[cid][3] = by_id[cid][3].replace("example.org", "example.net")
    by_id[5][2] = by_id[5][2] + "-Hughes"  # surname corrected
    new.append([41, "Grace", "Adeyemi", "grace.adeyemi41@example.org", "Eastholm", "member", "2025-06-20"])
    new.append([42, "Ivan", "Horvat", "ivan.horvat42@example.org", "Brackenridge", "trade", "2025-06-28"])
    return new


def orders(custs):
    town = {r[0]: r[4] for r in custs}
    days = sorted(between(0, 180) for _ in range(150))
    order_rows, line_rows = [], []
    for i, day in enumerate(days):
        oid = 1001 + i
        cid = between(1, 40)
        home = HOME_STORE.get(town[cid])
        store = home if home and rng.random() < 0.8 else between(1, 3)
        channel = "online" if rng.random() < 0.3 else "in-store"
        status = "cancelled" if rng.random() < 0.05 else "completed"
        order_rows.append([oid, cid, store, (date(2025, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=day)).isoformat(),
                           channel, pick(["card", "card", "cash", "account"]), status])
        line_rows += lines(oid)
    return order_rows, line_rows


def lines(oid, n=None):
    chosen = []
    for _ in range(n or between(1, 4)):
        p = pick(PRODUCTS)
        if p not in chosen:
            chosen.append(p)
    out = []
    for line_no, p in enumerate(chosen, 1):
        qty = between(10, 40) if p[0] == 10 else between(1, 5)
        out.append([oid, line_no, p[0], qty, p[4], pick([0, 0, 0, 10, 20])])
    return out


def daily_extract(day, first_oid, customer_ids, store_ids):
    """A flat sales extract, one row per order line, as a source system might send each night."""
    rows = []
    for k, (cid, sid) in enumerate(zip(customer_ids, store_ids)):
        oid = first_oid + k
        channel, payment = pick(["in-store", "online"]), pick(["card", "cash", "account"])
        for line in lines(oid, n=2):
            rows.append([line[0], line[1], day, cid, sid, line[2], line[3], line[4], line[5], channel, payment])
    return rows


def main():
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    custs = customers()
    order_rows, line_rows = orders(custs)
    write("stores.csv", ["store_id", "store_name", "town", "region", "opened"], STORES)
    write("categories.csv", ["category_id", "category_name", "department"], CATEGORIES)
    write("products.csv", ["product_id", "sku", "product_name", "category_id", "list_price"], PRODUCTS)
    write("customers.csv", ["customer_id", "first_name", "last_name", "email", "town", "segment", "joined"], custs)
    write("orders.csv", ["order_id", "customer_id", "store_id", "order_date", "channel", "payment", "status"],
          order_rows)
    write("order_lines.csv", ["order_id", "line_no", "product_id", "quantity", "unit_price", "discount_pct"],
          line_rows)
    write("customers_2025-07-01.csv",
          ["customer_id", "first_name", "last_name", "email", "town", "segment", "joined"], changed_customers(custs))
    header = ["order_id", "line_no", "order_date", "customer_id", "store_id", "product_id", "quantity",
              "unit_price", "discount_pct", "channel", "payment"]
    write("sales_2025-07-01.csv", header, daily_extract("2025-07-01", 1151, [3, 41, 12, 8, 30], [2, 2, 1, 3, 1]))
    write("sales_2025-07-02.csv", header, daily_extract("2025-07-02", 1156, [17, 99, 22, 5], [1, 2, 9, 3]))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Dimensional modelling: facts, dimensions and grain
modules.summary: Kimball's four-step design process, the kinds of fact table and measure, how to design dimensions, and the surrogate keys, conformed dimensions and bus matrix that tie a warehouse together.

lessons.title: The four-step design process and the grain
objectives: Apply Kimball's four design steps to a business process
Declare a fact table's grain and explain why it comes first
key_points: Kimball's four steps are: choose the business process, such as retail sales; declare the grain; identify the dimensions; and identify the facts. The order matters, because each step depends on the one before.
The grain states exactly what one row of the fact table represents, such as one row per order line, and every dimension and fact in the table must be true to it.
Choose the most atomic grain the source can provide: detailed rows can always be summarised later, but summarised rows can't answer questions about the detail they've lost.
Dimensions give a measurement its context (who, what, where, when and how), and facts are the numeric measurements of the process, such as quantity sold and net amount.

A common mistake is mixing grains in one table, such as an order-level delivery charge repeated on every order line, which double counts when summed; allocate it to the lines or give it its own fact table.

lessons.title: Fact tables and their measures
objectives: Distinguish transaction, periodic snapshot and accumulating snapshot fact tables
Classify measures as additive, semi-additive or non-additive
key_points: A transaction fact table has one row per event, such as an order line or a payment: the most common kind and the most detailed.

A periodic snapshot records a state at regular intervals, such as stock on hand per store at the end of each day; an accumulating snapshot has one row per process instance, such as an order, updated as it reaches milestones like shipped and delivered.

Additive facts, such as quantity and net amount, can be summed across every dimension; semi-additive facts, such as a stock level or an account balance, can be summed across stores but not across time, where you take the closing value or the average instead.
Non-additive facts, such as a unit price or a margin percentage, can't be summed at all: store the additive parts, such as revenue and cost, and calculate the ratio after summing.
A factless fact table records that an event happened or a relationship existed, with no measures, such as which students attended which classes; queries count its rows.
Fact tables are narrow and long, holding foreign keys to dimensions plus measures; a degenerate dimension, such as an order number, is a dimension key kept in the fact table with no table of its own.

lessons.title: Designing dimensions
objectives: Design dimension tables with descriptive attributes and flattened hierarchies
Build a date dimension, a junk dimension and role-playing dimensions
key_points: Dimension tables are wide and denormalised: they hold the descriptive text people filter and group by, such as product name, category and department, in one table, with hierarchies flattened into columns.

Every warehouse needs a date dimension, one row per day with attributes such as month name, quarter, weekday and holiday flags; a yyyymmdd integer key such as 20250318 is the usual exception to meaningless keys.

A junk dimension gathers low-cardinality flags and codes, such as sales channel and payment method, into one small table of their combinations, instead of cluttering the fact table or making many tiny dimensions.

A role-playing dimension is one physical dimension used in several roles, such as the date dimension joined as both order date and ship date, usually through views that give each role its own column names.
Use readable labels rather than codes in dimension attributes, and avoid nulls in attributes people filter on: use a value such as 'Unknown' or 'Not applicable' instead.

lessons.title: Surrogate keys, conformed dimensions and the bus matrix
objectives: Explain why dimensions use surrogate keys
Use conformed dimensions and a bus matrix to plan a warehouse
key_points: A surrogate key is a meaningless integer the warehouse assigns, such as product_key 7, while the source system's own identifier is kept as the natural, or durable, key.

Surrogate keys protect the warehouse from changes and clashes in source keys, let one natural key have several historical versions, and allow special rows such as an unknown member; integer joins are also compact and fast.

Conformed dimensions are shared by several fact tables with the same keys, attribute names and values, so measures from different processes, such as sales and stock, can be compared side by side, which is called drilling across.

The enterprise bus matrix lists business processes as rows and dimensions as columns, with a mark where a process uses a dimension; it shows which conformed dimensions to build first and which facts can be compared.
Build the warehouse one business process at a time against the bus matrix: each new fact table reuses the existing conformed dimensions instead of creating its own copies.

-- Lab 2: build the co-op's star schema from the OLTP tables (run oltp_schema.sql first).
-- Run with:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb build_star.sql   then   python run_sql.py shop.duckdb check_star.sql
-- Grain of fact_sales: one row per order line of a completed order.

-- dim_date: one row per day of 2025, keyed by a yyyymmdd integer
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_date AS
SELECT CAST(strftime(d, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER) AS date_key,
       CAST(d AS DATE)                        AS full_date,
       year(d)                                AS year,
       quarter(d)                             AS quarter,
       month(d)                               AS month,
       strftime(d, '%B')                      AS month_name,
       strftime(d, '%Y-%m')                   AS year_month,
       strftime(d, '%A')                      AS day_name,
       isodow(d) >= 6                         AS is_weekend
FROM range(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2026-01-01', INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS t(d);

-- dim_store: a surrogate key for each store
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_store AS
SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY store_id) AS store_key,
       store_id, store_name, town, region, opened
FROM stores;

-- TODO 1, dim_product: product_key (row_number() over product_id), product_id, sku, product_name,
-- category (the category's name) and department, joined in from categories, and list_price.

-- TODO 2, dim_customer: customer_key (row_number() over customer_id), customer_id,
-- full_name (first_name || ' ' || last_name), email, town, segment and joined.

-- TODO 3, dim_order_type: a junk dimension with one row for every combination of channel and payment
-- (CROSS JOIN the distinct values of each); order_type_key is row_number() over channel, payment.

-- TODO 4, fact_sales: one row per order line of a completed order, with
--   date_key, store_key, product_key, customer_key, order_type_key  (look each one up in its dimension)
--   order_id, line_no                                                (degenerate dimensions)
--   quantity, gross_amount, discount_amount, net_amount             (additive measures, DECIMAL(12, 2))
-- gross = quantity * unit_price; discount = gross * discount_pct / 100; net = gross - discount.

-- Checks for the star schema. Run with:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb check_star.sql

-- C1: rows in each table of the star
SELECT 'dim_date' AS table_name, count(*) AS row_count FROM dim_date
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_store', count(*) FROM dim_store
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_product', count(*) FROM dim_product
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_customer', count(*) FROM dim_customer
UNION ALL SELECT 'dim_order_type', count(*) FROM dim_order_type
UNION ALL SELECT 'fact_sales', count(*) FROM fact_sales;

-- C2: the grain is unique, one row per order line
SELECT count(*) AS duplicate_lines
FROM (SELECT order_id, line_no FROM fact_sales GROUP BY order_id, line_no HAVING count(*) > 1);

-- C3: every fact row finds its dimension rows (all zeros)
SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE d.date_key IS NULL)      AS missing_dates,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE s.store_key IS NULL)     AS missing_stores,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE p.product_key IS NULL)   AS missing_products,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE c.customer_key IS NULL)  AS missing_customers
FROM fact_sales AS f
LEFT JOIN dim_date AS d USING (date_key)
LEFT JOIN dim_store AS s USING (store_key)
LEFT JOIN dim_product AS p USING (product_key)
LEFT JOIN dim_customer AS c USING (customer_key);

-- C4: the star reconciles with the source system
SELECT (SELECT sum(net_amount) FROM fact_sales) AS star_net,
       (SELECT CAST(sum(l.quantity * l.unit_price * (100 - l.discount_pct) / 100) AS DECIMAL(12, 2))
        FROM order_lines AS l JOIN orders AS o USING (order_id)
        WHERE o.status = 'completed') AS source_net,
       (SELECT sum(gross_amount) - sum(discount_amount) - sum(net_amount) FROM fact_sales) AS gross_less_discount_less_net;

-- C5: net revenue by department and quarter, from the star
SELECT p.department, d.quarter, sum(f.net_amount) AS net_revenue
FROM fact_sales AS f
JOIN dim_product AS p USING (product_key)
JOIN dim_date AS d USING (date_key)
GROUP BY p.department, d.quarter
ORDER BY p.department, d.quarter;

-- C6: weekend share of net revenue by channel
SELECT ot.channel,
       sum(f.net_amount) AS net_revenue,
       sum(f.net_amount) FILTER (WHERE d.is_weekend) AS weekend_net
FROM fact_sales AS f
JOIN dim_order_type AS ot USING (order_type_key)
JOIN dim_date AS d USING (date_key)
GROUP BY ot.channel
ORDER BY ot.channel;

hints: If fact_sales has 368 rows, the cancelled orders' lines are still in: filter on o.status = 'completed'.
If star_net is bigger than source_net, a join is multiplying rows: each dimension must have one row per natural key, and dim_order_type must be joined on both channel and payment.
dim_order_type is (SELECT DISTINCT channel FROM orders) CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT payment FROM orders), with row_number() for the key.

modules.title: Slowly changing dimensions
modules.summary: How dimensions keep up with a changing world: SCD types 0, 1, 2 and 3, the mechanics of type 2 versions, and the SQL that applies changes and finds the right version when facts arrive.

lessons.title: Why dimensions change, and the SCD types
objectives: Explain the slowly changing dimension types and what each does to history
Choose a type for each attribute of a dimension
key_points: Dimension attributes change: customers move, products are recategorised and stores are reorganised; a slowly changing dimension (SCD) technique decides, attribute by attribute, what happens to history when they do.

Type 0 keeps the original value for ever, such as the channel a customer first signed up through; type 1 overwrites the old value, so every past fact now reports the new value and the history is lost.
Type 2 adds a new row, a new version with its own surrogate key, so facts recorded before the change still point to the old version and reports show history as it was.
Type 3 adds a column for the previous value, such as previous_region, which lets reports compare the old and new values side by side but keeps only one step of history.

Use type 1 for corrections and attributes whose history nobody needs, such as a mistyped surname, and type 2 for attributes that change how history should be reported, such as a customer's region; one dimension usually mixes both.
Type 6 combines types 1, 2 and 3: type 2 versions, plus a current-value column overwritten on every version, so reports can show either the value at the time or the value today.

lessons.title: Type 2 mechanics: versions, dates and lookups
objectives: Describe the columns a type 2 dimension needs
Look up the version that was current when a fact happened
key_points: A type 2 dimension keeps the natural key on every version and adds a validity range, valid_from and valid_to (also called effective and expiry dates), and an is_current flag.

Half-open ranges avoid gaps and overlaps: a version applies from valid_from up to but not including valid_to, the next version starts on that same date, and the current version's valid_to is a far-future date such as 9999-12-31 rather than NULL.
Each natural key must have exactly one current row and no overlapping ranges, and both rules are worth checking after every load.

When facts are loaded, the lookup joins on the natural key and the fact's date, order_date >= valid_from AND order_date < valid_to, which finds the version current at the time, even for a fact that arrives late.
Reporting through the fact's surrogate key shows history as it was; joining through the natural key to the current row shows all of history by today's attributes, as it is.
Leaving the date condition out of the lookup joins each fact to every version of its customer, which silently multiplies rows and revenue.

lessons.title: Applying changes with SQL
objectives: Detect changed rows by comparing a staged extract with the dimension
Apply type 1 and type 2 changes in a safe, repeatable order
key_points: A change load compares a staged extract with the dimension's current rows on the natural key; IS DISTINCT FROM compares safely when either side can be NULL, where <> returns NULL and misses the change.

Apply type 1 attributes first, on every version; then close the current version of rows whose type 2 attributes changed; then insert a new current version for each staged key that has no current row, which covers both changed and new customers.
Run the steps in one transaction, so a failure can't leave a customer without a current version, and write them so that applying the same extract twice changes nothing the second time.
New versions' surrogate keys come from a sequence or identity column, or the current maximum key plus row_number(); never reuse or renumber existing keys, because facts point at them.

PostgreSQL 15 and later and DuckDB 1.4 and later also support MERGE, which matches, updates and inserts in one statement; a type 2 change still needs both the old version closed and the new one inserted.
For wide dimensions, comparing a hash of the type 2 columns, such as md5 of the values joined with a separator, is a common shortcut for spotting which rows changed.

-- Lab 3 set-up: a type 2 customer dimension, a small sales fact and the new customer extract.
-- Run oltp_schema.sql first, then:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb scd_setup.sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_customer (
    customer_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,   -- surrogate key: one per version
    customer_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,      -- natural (durable) key from the source system
    first_name   VARCHAR NOT NULL,      -- type 1: a correction overwrites every version
    last_name    VARCHAR NOT NULL,      -- type 1
    email        VARCHAR NOT NULL,      -- type 1
    town         VARCHAR NOT NULL,      -- type 2: a change starts a new version
    segment      VARCHAR NOT NULL,      -- type 2
    valid_from   DATE NOT NULL,         -- first day this version applies
    valid_to     DATE NOT NULL,         -- first day it no longer applies; 9999-12-31 if current
    is_current   BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO dim_customer
SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id), customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, town, segment,
       DATE '1900-01-01', DATE '9999-12-31', true
FROM customers;

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE fact_sales (
    date_key     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    order_id     INTEGER NOT NULL,
    line_no      INTEGER NOT NULL,
    customer_key INTEGER NOT NULL,
    net_amount   DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO fact_sales
SELECT CAST(strftime(o.order_date, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER), o.order_id, l.line_no, c.customer_key,
       CAST(l.quantity * l.unit_price * (100 - l.discount_pct) / 100 AS DECIMAL(12, 2))
FROM order_lines AS l
JOIN orders AS o USING (order_id)
JOIN dim_customer AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed';

-- The customer extract the source system sent on 2025-07-01
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE stg_customer AS
SELECT * FROM read_csv('data/customers_2025-07-01.csv', header = true);

-- Before the change
SELECT count(*) AS dim_rows, (SELECT count(*) FROM stg_customer) AS staged_rows,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM fact_sales) AS fact_rows
FROM dim_customer;

-- Lab 3: apply the 2025-07-01 customer extract (stg_customer) to the type 2 dim_customer.
-- Run with:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb scd_apply.sql

-- Step 1 (type 1): overwrite corrected names and emails on every version of the customer
UPDATE dim_customer AS d
SET first_name = s.first_name, last_name = s.last_name, email = s.email
FROM stg_customer AS s
WHERE d.customer_id = s.customer_id
  AND (d.first_name IS DISTINCT FROM s.first_name
       OR d.last_name IS DISTINCT FROM s.last_name
       OR d.email IS DISTINCT FROM s.email);

-- TODO Step 2 (type 2): close the current version of each customer whose town or segment changed:
-- set valid_to to DATE '2025-07-01' and is_current to false. Compare with IS DISTINCT FROM.

-- TODO Step 3: insert a new current version for every staged customer that has no current row now
-- (the ones step 2 closed, and brand-new customers): a new customer_key (the current maximum plus
-- row_number() over customer_id), the staged attributes, valid_from DATE '2025-07-01',
-- valid_to DATE '9999-12-31' and is_current true. A LEFT JOIN to the current rows finds them.

-- Lab 3: load the 2025-07-01 sales extract with a point-in-time lookup of the customer.
-- Run with:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb load_july.sql
INSERT INTO fact_sales (date_key, order_id, line_no, customer_key, net_amount)
SELECT CAST(strftime(x.order_date, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER), x.order_id, x.line_no, c.customer_key,
       CAST(x.quantity * x.unit_price * (100 - x.discount_pct) / 100 AS DECIMAL(12, 2))
FROM read_csv('data/sales_2025-07-01.csv', header = true) AS x
JOIN dim_customer AS c
  ON c.customer_id = x.customer_id
 -- TODO: and the version that was valid on the order date (valid_to is exclusive)
;

-- Rows loaded for 2025-07-01
SELECT count(*) AS july_rows FROM fact_sales WHERE date_key = 20250701;

-- Checks for the type 2 customer dimension. Run with:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb check_scd.sql

-- S1: versions in the dimension
SELECT count(*) AS total_rows,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_current) AS current_rows,
       count(DISTINCT customer_id) AS customers
FROM dim_customer;

-- S2: the history of five customers
SELECT customer_id, customer_key, last_name, email, town, segment, valid_from, valid_to, is_current
FROM dim_customer
WHERE customer_id IN (3, 5, 8, 12, 41)
ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from;

-- S3: rules every type 2 dimension keeps (both should be 0)
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM dim_customer GROUP BY customer_id
                         HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE is_current) <> 1)) AS customers_without_one_current_row,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM dim_customer AS a
   JOIN dim_customer AS b
     ON a.customer_id = b.customer_id AND a.customer_key < b.customer_key
    AND a.valid_from < b.valid_to AND b.valid_from < a.valid_to) AS overlapping_versions;

-- S4: each July order points at the customer version current on its date
SELECT DISTINCT f.order_id, c.customer_id, c.customer_key, c.town, c.valid_from
FROM fact_sales AS f
JOIN dim_customer AS c USING (customer_key)
WHERE f.date_key = 20250701
ORDER BY f.order_id;

-- S5: net revenue by town, as it was at the time of each sale and as it is now
WITH as_was AS (
    SELECT c.town, sum(f.net_amount) AS net
    FROM fact_sales AS f JOIN dim_customer AS c USING (customer_key)
    GROUP BY c.town),
as_is AS (
    SELECT cur.town, sum(f.net_amount) AS net
    FROM fact_sales AS f
    JOIN dim_customer AS c USING (customer_key)
    JOIN dim_customer AS cur ON cur.customer_id = c.customer_id AND cur.is_current
    GROUP BY cur.town)
SELECT town, as_was.net AS as_was_net, as_is.net AS as_is_net
FROM as_was FULL JOIN as_is USING (town)
ORDER BY town;

hints: If july_rows is 13 rather than 9, the lookup is missing its date condition, so every version of customers 3 and 12 matched.
Step 3's LEFT JOIN must match current rows only (AND d.is_current); otherwise the four customers step 2 closed still find their old row, get no new version, and S3 reports them.
The new keys can be (SELECT max(customer_key) FROM dim_customer) + row_number() OVER (ORDER BY s.customer_id).

modules.title: Star or snowflake, aggregates and physical design
modules.summary: When to normalise a dimension and when not to, how aggregate tables and materialised views speed up common questions without changing the answers, and the partitioning, sorting and file choices that keep large fact tables fast.

lessons.title: Star and snowflake schemas
objectives: Compare star and snowflake schemas and choose between them
Handle a many-to-many relationship with a bridge table
key_points: In a star schema each dimension is one denormalised table joined directly to the fact table; in a snowflake schema dimensions are normalised into several tables, such as product, category and department, joined in a chain.

Stars are simpler to query and understand and need fewer joins; the repeated text in a denormalised dimension costs little, because dimensions are small next to facts and columnar storage compresses repeated values well.

Snowflaking can be justified for a large, separately maintained group of attributes hanging off a dimension (an outrigger, such as demographics attached to customer), or when a tool needs it, but it rarely makes queries faster.
Kimball's guidance is to snowflake sparingly, if at all; built correctly, both designs give the same answers, so the choice is about usability and maintenance.

When one fact relates to many values of a dimension, such as a hospital visit with several diagnoses, a bridge table between them holds the pairs, often with a weighting factor so totals aren't double counted.

lessons.title: Aggregate tables and materialised views
objectives: Design aggregate fact tables that reconcile with the base fact
Compare summary tables with materialised views, and report subtotals with ROLLUP
key_points: An aggregate fact table stores the base facts summarised to a coarser grain, such as month by store by category, so frequent queries scan far fewer rows.

Aggregates join to shrunken dimensions: rolled-up versions of the base dimensions with only the attributes at the aggregate's grain, such as a month dimension, using the same attribute names and values.

An aggregate must reconcile exactly with its base fact, with the same totals and row counts, checked after every refresh; only additive measures can be summed into it, so store counts and sums and calculate ratios afterwards.

In PostgreSQL, CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores a query's result and REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW recomputes it; CONCURRENTLY lets readers carry on during the refresh if the view has a unique index. DuckDB has no materialised views, so a rebuilt summary table does the job.
Aggregate navigation sends each query to the smallest aggregate that can answer it; some BI tools and warehouses do it automatically, otherwise report queries name the aggregate directly.
GROUP BY ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS calculate subtotals and grand totals in one query, and the GROUPING() function tells a subtotal row from a detail row.

lessons.title: Physical design: partitions, sorting and files
objectives: Choose partitioning and a sort order for a large fact table
Write and query partitioned Parquet with DuckDB
key_points: Partitioning splits a large table into parts by a column, usually a date, so a query filtering on that column reads only the matching parts (partition pruning), and a whole partition can be loaded, replaced or deleted as a unit.
Keep partitions coarse enough to be a sensible size: partitioning a small table by day, or by a column with many distinct values, makes many tiny files that slow queries down.
Sorting or clustering data by commonly filtered columns narrows each block's min-max range, so zone maps skip more blocks; cloud warehouses offer this as clustering keys or sort keys.

Row stores such as PostgreSQL rely on B-tree indexes for selective lookups and support declarative partitioning; columnar warehouses rely mainly on scans, compression, pruning and statistics rather than indexes.

DuckDB's COPY ... TO with PARTITION_BY writes Hive-style folders such as year=2025/month=3, and read_parquet with hive_partitioning = true turns the folder names back into columns and prunes partitions using a query's filters.

-- The co-op's reference star schema (the module 2 lab's solution), built from the OLTP tables.
-- Run oltp_schema.sql first, then:  python run_sql.py shop.duckdb build_star_reference.sql

-- dim_date: one row per day of 2025, keyed by a yyyymmdd integer
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_date AS
SELECT CAST(strftime(d, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER) AS date_key,
       CAST(d AS DATE)                        AS full_date,
       year(d)                                AS year,
       quarter(d)                             AS quarter,
       month(d)                               AS month,
       strftime(d, '%B')                      AS month_name,
       strftime(d, '%Y-%m')                   AS year_month,
       strftime(d, '%A')                      AS day_name,
       isodow(d) >= 6                         AS is_weekend
FROM range(DATE '2025-01-01', DATE '2026-01-01', INTERVAL 1 DAY) AS t(d);

-- dim_store: a surrogate key for each store
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_store AS
SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY store_id) AS store_key,
       store_id, store_name, town, region, opened
FROM stores;

-- dim_product: the category and department are folded in (denormalised)
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_product AS
SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY p.product_id) AS product_key,
       p.product_id, p.sku, p.product_name, c.category_name AS category, c.department, p.list_price
FROM products AS p
JOIN categories AS c USING (category_id);

-- dim_customer: one row per customer (type 1 for now; module 3 adds history)
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_customer AS
SELECT row_number() OVER (ORDER BY customer_id) AS customer_key,
       customer_id, first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name, email, town, segment, joined
FROM customers;

-- dim_order_type: a junk dimension for two low-cardinality flags
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dim_order_type AS

modules.title: Loading the warehouse, and the lakehouse
modules.summary: Load patterns that keep a warehouse right night after night (incremental and idempotent loads, unknown and inferred members, audit columns), and where open table formats, lakehouses and cloud warehouses fit around a dimensional model.

lessons.title: Incremental, idempotent loads
objectives: Design loads that pick up only new data and can safely run twice
Handle late-arriving dimension rows and keys that can't be found
key_points: Full reloads are simple but slow down as data grows; incremental loads pick up only what's new, tracked by a high-water mark such as the latest updated_at value loaded, or by a log of the files already processed.

An idempotent load gives the same result however many times it runs: inside one transaction, delete what an earlier run loaded from the same file or date and insert it again (delete-insert), or MERGE on the fact's natural key.

Load dimensions before facts, so fact rows can find their surrogate keys; a fact whose key can't be found gets the unknown member, often key -1, rather than being dropped, because an inner join silently loses revenue.

A late-arriving dimension row, such as a sale for a customer the customer extract hasn't sent yet, gets an inferred member: a placeholder row with the natural key and an is_inferred flag, filled in with a type 1 update when the details arrive.
Audit columns and a load log, such as the source file, load time and rows loaded, trace every fact back to its batch, so you can reconcile counts and re-run or remove one batch.

lessons.title: From warehouse to lakehouse: open table formats
objectives: Explain what an open table format adds to files in object storage
Describe how a lakehouse relates to a dimensional warehouse
key_points: A data lake keeps files, often Parquet, in object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage or Google Cloud Storage; plain files have no transactions, so a reader can see a half-written change, and nothing records a table's schema or history.

Open table formats, Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake and Apache Hudi, add a metadata layer over the data files that records which files make up each version (snapshot) of a table, giving atomic commits, schema evolution and time travel.

Because the format is open, several engines, such as Apache Spark, Trino, Apache Flink and DuckDB, can work with the same tables, with storage and compute separated; each engine's read and write support differs by format and version.
Updates and deletes either rewrite the affected files (copy-on-write) or write small delete files that readers merge in (merge-on-read), so tables with frequent small changes need regular compaction.

A lakehouse uses these tables to give a data lake warehouse features, and dimensional modelling still applies on top, often in medallion layers: bronze for raw data, silver for cleaned and conformed data, and gold for facts, dimensions and aggregates.
Table formats make warehouse load patterns easier on a lake: MERGE applies upserts and type 2 changes atomically, and snapshots let you audit a bad load or roll it back.

lessons.title: Dimensional models in today's data stack
objectives: Place dimensional modelling in a modern ELT stack
Weigh a star schema against one big wide table
key_points: Cloud data warehouses such as Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift and Microsoft Fabric separate storage from compute and store data by column, and the dimensional techniques in this course apply to all of them.

In an ELT stack, raw data lands in staging tables or files and SQL transformations build the dimensional layer inside the warehouse; tools such as dbt manage those SQL models with their dependencies, tests and documentation.

One big table pre-joins a fact with its dimensions into a single wide table: easy for some tools to query, but it repeats dimension values on every row and must be rebuilt when a type 1 attribute changes, so many teams build wide tables from a star rather than instead of one.
A semantic layer, in a BI tool or a separate service, defines measures such as net revenue once on top of the dimensional model, so every report calculates them the same way.
Whatever the stack, the habits that keep a warehouse trusted are the same: a declared grain, conformed dimensions, tested loads and numbers that reconcile with the source systems.

"""Load nightly sales extracts into the co-op's star schema: incremental, idempotent and audited.

Usage:
    python load_sales.py shop.duckdb data/sales_2025-07-01.csv   # load (or reload) one file
    python load_sales.py shop.duckdb --pending                    # load every file not loaded yet
    python load_sales.py shop.duckdb --report                     # print the load report
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb

INSERT_FACTS = """
INSERT INTO fact_sales (date_key, store_key, product_key, customer_key, order_type_key, order_id, line_no,
                        quantity, gross_amount, discount_amount, net_amount, source_file)
SELECT CAST(strftime(x.order_date, '%Y%m%d') AS INTEGER),
       s.store_key, p.product_key, c.customer_key, ot.order_type_key,
       x.order_id, x.line_no, x.quantity,
       CAST(x.quantity * x.unit_price AS DECIMAL(12, 2)),
       CAST(x.quantity * x.unit_price * x.discount_pct / 100 AS DECIMAL(12, 2)),
       CAST(x.quantity * x.unit_price * (100 - x.discount_pct) / 100 AS DECIMAL(12, 2)),
       ?
FROM stg_sales AS x
-- TODO 1: these inner joins silently drop any line whose store, product, customer or order type
-- isn't in its dimension. Make them LEFT JOINs and coalesce each missing key to -1, the unknown member.
JOIN dim_store AS s ON s.store_id = x.store_id
JOIN dim_product AS p ON p.product_id = x.product_id
JOIN dim_customer AS c ON c.customer_id = x.customer_id
JOIN dim_order_type AS ot ON ot.channel = x.channel AND ot.payment = x.payment
"""


def prepare(con):
    """Add the audit column, the inferred flag, the load log and an unknown member in each dimension.
    Every statement is safe to run again."""
    con.execute("ALTER TABLE fact_sales ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS source_file VARCHAR DEFAULT 'initial load'")
    con.execute("ALTER TABLE dim_customer ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS is_inferred BOOLEAN DEFAULT false")
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS load_log (file_name VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, rows_loaded INTEGER, "
                "loaded_at TIMESTAMP)")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO dim_store SELECT -1, -1, 'Unknown store', 'Unknown', 'Unknown', NULL "
                "WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim_store WHERE store_key = -1)")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO dim_product SELECT -1, -1, 'UNKNOWN', 'Unknown product', 'Unknown', 'Unknown', NULL "
                "WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim_product WHERE product_key = -1)")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO dim_customer SELECT -1, -1, 'Unknown customer', 'unknown', 'Unknown', 'Unknown', "
                "NULL, false WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_key = -1)")
    con.execute("INSERT INTO dim_order_type SELECT -1, 'unknown', 'unknown' "
                "WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim_order_type WHERE order_type_key = -1)")


def add_inferred_customers(con):
    """A customer in the extract who isn't in dim_customer yet (a late-arriving dimension row)
    gets an inferred member now; the customer extract fills in the details later."""
    # TODO 2: insert one inferred member row for each distinct customer_id in stg_sales that isn't in
    # dim_customer: a new customer_key (the current max plus row_number()), the customer_id,
    # full_name 'Inferred customer', email 'unknown', town and segment 'Unknown', joined NULL and
    # is_inferred true. Return how many rows were inserted:  con.execute(...).fetchone()[0]
    return 0


def load_file(con, path):
    """Load one extract inside a transaction: delete what an earlier run loaded from this file,
    insert it again and record the load, so running it twice gives the same result."""
    path = Path(path)
    con.execute("BEGIN TRANSACTION")
    try:
        con.execute("CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP TABLE stg_sales AS SELECT * FROM read_csv(?, header = true)",
                    [str(path)])
        inferred = add_inferred_customers(con)
        # TODO 3: make a re-run safe. Before inserting, delete the fact rows an earlier run loaded from
        # this file (source_file = path.name) and keep the count in replaced. After inserting, replace
        # this file's row in load_log with (file name, rows loaded, current_timestamp).
        replaced = 0
        loaded = con.execute(INSERT_FACTS, [path.name]).fetchone()[0]
        con.execute("COMMIT")
    except Exception:
        con.execute("ROLLBACK")
        raise
    print(f"{path.name}: {loaded} rows loaded, {replaced} replaced, {inferred} inferred customers")


def pending(con, folder):
    """The extracts in the folder that the load log hasn't recorded yet, oldest first."""
    done = {row[0] for row in con.execute("SELECT file_name FROM load_log").fetchall()}
    return [p for p in sorted(Path(folder).glob("sales_*.csv")) if p.name not in done]


def report(con):
    facts, net = con.execute("SELECT count(*), sum(net_amount) FROM fact_sales").fetchone()
    print(f"fact_sales: {facts} rows, net {net}")
    for name, value in con.execute("""
        SELECT 'rows with an unknown store', count(*) FROM fact_sales WHERE store_key = -1
        UNION ALL SELECT 'inferred customers', count(*) FROM dim_customer WHERE is_inferred
        UNION ALL SELECT 'files in load_log', count(*) FROM load_log""").fetchall():
        print(f"{name}: {value}")


def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        sys.exit(__doc__)
    con = duckdb.connect(sys.argv[1])
    prepare(con)
    if sys.argv[2] == "--report":
        report(con)
    elif sys.argv[2] == "--pending":
        files = pending(con, "data")
        if not files:
            print("Nothing to load")
        for path in files:
            load_file(con, path)
    else:
        load_file(con, sys.argv[2])
    con.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: coalesce(s.store_key, -1) gives the unknown member's key when the LEFT JOIN finds no store.
DuckDB returns how many rows a DELETE or INSERT changed: con.execute(sql, params).fetchone()[0].
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM dim_customer) finds the customers to infer.
Keep the DELETE, the INSERT and the load_log change between BEGIN TRANSACTION and COMMIT, so a failure halfway leaves the warehouse as it was.

project.title: Build a medicine-supply warehouse for rural clinics
project.brief: A district health office wants to know which clinics are about to run out of essential medicines, how quickly suppliers deliver, and how dispensing changes over time. Design and build its warehouse in DuckDB (or PostgreSQL) from the extracts that make_clinic_data.py writes: clinics, medicines, suppliers, daily dispensing, weekly stock counts and purchase orders, plus a clinic change file dated 2025-04-01. Model three business processes with conformed clinic, medicine and date dimensions: dispensing as a transaction fact, stock on hand as a weekly periodic snapshot (a semi-additive measure), and purchase orders as an accumulating snapshot with ordered, shipped and received dates (a role-playing date dimension). Treat clinic_type as type 2 (Lowveld was upgraded to a health centre) and clinic_name and district as type 1 corrections. Load everything with scripts you can re-run from scratch, build at least one aggregate, prove every table reconciles with its source, answer the office's questions in SQL, and explain your design.
deliverables: A bus matrix (business processes by dimensions) and a diagram or description of each star, with each fact table's grain stated in one sentence
DDL and load scripts (SQL or Python) that build every dimension and fact from the CSV files and can be re-run from scratch
Clinic history applied from clinic_changes_2025-04-01.csv, with dispensing facts pointing at the clinic version valid on each date
Reconciliation queries showing each fact's row count and quantity total match the source files, plus checks for a unique grain and orphan keys
An aggregate table, such as weekly dispensing by clinic and therapeutic class, that reconciles with its base fact

SQL answers, with results, to five questions: weekly dispensing by therapeutic class; closing stock on the last count date by clinic and medicine; average days from order to receipt by supplier; the purchase orders still open; and Lowveld's dispensing as it was and as it is
A design note of one to two pages explaining the grains, the SCD choices, how the stock snapshot must be summarised, and what you'd change for a much larger dataset

files.content:
"""Write source data for the capstone: medicine supply at a district's rural clinics.

Writes CSV files to clinic_data/. Only random.Random(7).random() is used, so every
computer gets exactly the same rows.   Run:  python make_clinic_data.py
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path("clinic_data")
START = date(2025, 1, 6)  # a Monday; the data covers 26 weeks
END = START + timedelta(weeks=25, days=4)  # the last day in the data, a Friday
rng = random.Random(7)


def between(lo, hi):
    return lo + int(rng.random() * (hi - lo + 1))


CLINICS = [(1, "Lowveld Health Post", "Lowveld", "health post"),
           (2, "Riverbend Clinic", "Riverbend", "health centre"),
           (3, "Hilltop Clinic", "Hilltop", "health centre"),
           (4, "Saltpan Health Post", "Saltpan", "health post"),
           (5, "District Hospital", "Central", "hospital")]
MEDICINES = [  # medicine_id, code, name, therapeutic class, form, units per pack
    (1, "AMX250", "Amoxicillin 250mg", "Antibiotic", "capsule", 100),
    (2, "PCM500", "Paracetamol 500mg", "Analgesic", "tablet", 100),
    (3, "ORS", "Oral rehydration salts", "Rehydration", "sachet", 50),
    (4, "ZNC20", "Zinc 20mg", "Supplement", "tablet", 100),
    (5, "MET500", "Metformin 500mg", "Diabetes", "tablet", 60),
    (6, "AML5", "Amlodipine 5mg", "Hypertension", "tablet", 30),
    (7, "SAL100", "Salbutamol inhaler", "Respiratory", "inhaler", 1),
    (8, "IRF", "Iron and folic acid", "Supplement", "tablet", 100)]
SUPPLIERS = [(1, "Central Medical Stores"), (2, "Valley Pharma Distributors"), (3, "Northern Health Supplies")]
SIZE = {"health post": 1, "health centre": 2, "hospital": 4}


def write(name, header, rows):
    with open(OUT / name, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(header)
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"{name}: {len(rows)} rows")


def main():
    OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    dispensing, counts, orders = [], [], []
    stock = {(c[0], m[0]): 400 * SIZE[c[3]] for c in CLINICS for m in MEDICINES}
    for week in range(26):
        monday = START + timedelta(weeks=week)
        for c in CLINICS:
            for m in MEDICINES:
                key = (c[0], m[0])
                for day in range(5):
                    qty = between(0, 12) * SIZE[c[3]]
                    if qty and stock[key] >= qty:
                        stock[key] -= qty
                        dispensing.append([len(dispensing) + 1, c[0], m[0],
                                           (monday + timedelta(days=day)).isoformat(), qty])
                counts.append([(monday + timedelta(days=4)).isoformat(), c[0], m[0], stock[key]])
                if stock[key] < 150 * SIZE[c[3]] and rng.random() < 0.7:
                    qty = 300 * SIZE[c[3]]
                    shipped = monday + timedelta(days=between(2, 6))
                    received = shipped + timedelta(days=between(1, 9))
                    po = [5000 + len(orders) + 1, c[0], 1 + int(rng.random() * 3), m[0], qty,
                          monday.isoformat(), shipped.isoformat(), received.isoformat()]
                    if received <= END:
                        stock[key] += qty
                    else:  # still open when the data ends
                        po[7] = ""
                        if shipped > END:
                            po[6] = ""
                    orders.append(po)
    last_monday = START + timedelta(weeks=25)
    orders.append([5000 + len(orders) + 1, 3, 2, 7, 60, last_monday.isoformat(),
                   (last_monday + timedelta(days=2)).isoformat(), ""])  # shipped, not yet received
    orders.append([5000 + len(orders) + 1, 4, 1, 3, 300, last_monday.isoformat(), "", ""])  # not yet shipped
    write("clinics.csv", ["clinic_id", "clinic_name", "district", "clinic_type"], CLINICS)
    write("clinic_changes_2025-04-01.csv", ["clinic_id", "clinic_name", "district", "clinic_type"],
          [(1, "Lowveld Clinic", "Lowveld", "health centre"), (4, "Saltpan Health Post", "Saltpan East",
                                                                 "health post")])
    write("medicines.csv", ["medicine_id", "code", "medicine_name", "therapeutic_class", "form", "pack_size"],
          MEDICINES)
    write("suppliers.csv", ["supplier_id", "supplier_name"], SUPPLIERS)
    write("dispensing.csv", ["dispense_id", "clinic_id", "medicine_id", "dispensed_date", "quantity"], dispensing)
    write("stock_counts.csv", ["count_date", "clinic_id", "medicine_id", "quantity_on_hand"], counts)
    write("purchase_orders.csv", ["po_id", "clinic_id", "supplier_id", "medicine_id", "quantity", "ordered_date",
                                  "shipped_date", "received_date"], orders)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
